idiom_name: struct per row + person_* functions over sqlite3/libpq prepared statements
implementation_notes: C has no objects, so the gateway is a struct whose fields mirror the columns plus a naming convention - person_find / person_insert / person_update - taking the database handle as a parameter. sqlite3_prepare_v2, sqlite3_bind_*, sqlite3_step and the sqlite3_column_* family (or PQprepare/PQexecPrepared on PostgreSQL) do the work, and the finder is a function that fills a caller-provided struct, returning a status code instead of an object. Nothing replaces the classic structure here: the full role set (fields, finder, insert, update, delete) is hand-written, which is normal in C because there is neither reflection nor an ORM culture to generate it.
code_sketch:
typedef struct { long id; char last[32]; char first[32]; int deps; } person_row;

int person_find(sqlite3 *db, long id, person_row *out);   /* SELECT ... WHERE id=? */
int person_insert(sqlite3 *db, person_row *r);            /* INSERT + last_insert_rowid() */
int person_update(sqlite3 *db, const person_row *r);      /* UPDATE ... WHERE id=? */
int person_delete(sqlite3 *db, long id);                  /* DELETE ... WHERE id=? */
pitfalls: Every prepared statement must be finalised (sqlite3_finalize) on all paths, including error exits, or the connection leaks statement handles.
The char* returned by sqlite3_column_text points into the statement's buffer and is invalidated by the next sqlite3_step - copy it immediately.
Return codes are easy to ignore: an unchecked SQLITE_BUSY or constraint violation silently produces a half-applied update.
A connection or statement is not shared across threads unless SQLite is compiled with serialised threading; per-thread handles are the safe default.
